text:
Enjoy today, because it's the last mild one for a while. It's mostly cloudy with a high near 64, and a spotty shower is possible, though most of the day stays dry. Tonight cools to around 45, with a few sprinkles possible toward dawn.

Saturday is where the pattern flips. A slow-moving low settles in, and the high only gets to about 54, with some of the models closer to 50. Rain is likely all day, but the morning is light, under a tenth of an inch. The steadier rain arrives around lunchtime and peaks from about 2 to 4 in the afternoon, so do your errands early and keep the umbrella close after noon. Saturday night is the soaker, a quarter to half inch, with a low near 37. The latest guidance has trended wetter for us, so a bigger total, even up to an inch, isn't off the table if the low strengthens quickly. A little wet snow may mix in on the highest hills overnight, but I'd expect plain rain down here.

Sunday starts wet, with rain tapering off around 1, then a few leftover showers and a brief break. It stays mostly cloudy. The forecasters say 52 for the high, but the models lean cooler, so I'd bet on the upper 40s to low 50s. Showers return Sunday night, and next week looks chilly. Sunday afternoon is your best window for a walk.

KEY MESSAGE 1: An active weather pattern will be present through the next several days as shortwave troughs move through our region. The first of these is a slow mover; an upper level low will cross New York and Vermont from Saturday afternoon through Sunday morning, when highest chances of rain generally are on the table. To start with for today, we are within a dry slot ahead of the first upper level low and a plume of deeper moisture along a developing coastal front. It appears on the northwestern fringe of this plume showers tracking over southeastern New York will likely slide through southern and eastern Vermont, with a batch of showers arriving by noon and exiting soon after. As a wave of low pressure develops over southern New England, somewhat heavier showers will develop; there remains quite a bit of spread with how far west the rain will get. As such, have maintained roughly 40-60% PoPs over eastern Vermont with a more uncertain 0.1 - 0.3" of rain than typical in this time range. Meanwhile, shower chances will increase Friday afternoon over western portions of northern New York as strong upper level divergence and some near surface convergent flow develops ahead of the aforementioned upper level low. Showers in this area will be light but persistent for much of the weekend, especially towards southern St. Lawrence, Franklin, and Essex counties, and will gradually expand eastward into the south central Vermont. As the upper level low crosses to our south Saturday night, sufficient cooling for a changeover to snow in higher elevations is becoming a bit more likely. Probabilities of at least some snow mixing in with rain, even down to elevations as low as 1000 to 1500 feet if precipitation is heavy enough, are above 20%, especially over northeastern portions of Vermont and the northwestern Adirondacks. In a reasonable high end scenario given a timeframe falling during the nighttime hours, up to a couple inches of wet snow could accumulate in some towns above 1500 feet. The northward extent of rain showers, and potential for steadier rain particularly in the Saturday afternoon through Sunday morning timeframe, remains uncertain. The latest guidance has trended wetter in northern areas including north central and northwestern Vermont. The potential for a good soaking rain, with rainfall amounts in the range of 0.5"-1", would be tied to a more rapidly deepening surface low pressure area in the Gulf of Maine and an associated deformation zone across western Vermont/northeastern New York that is favored due to terrain enhanced convergence. Precipitation chances generally look at their minimum for the weekend later Sunday as brief ridging builds in before another shortwave trough quickly approaches for Sunday night. On Monday, the most noteworthy part of the forecast may be related to seasonably gusty northwest winds as another trough swings through with typical cold season advection.
